exercise1.prompt: Pivot Tables: The shape of the grid

hiddenCases.name: one subject and one year is a single cell
the grid has a column per distinct year

exercise1.hint: index is what goes down the side, columns is what goes across the top, values is what fills the cells. The shape is distinct subjects by distinct years.

exercise2.prompt: Pivot Tables: How many pairs never happened

hiddenCases.name: a full grid has no gaps
a single cell grid is full
the count is a plain int

exercise2.hint: Pivot with aggfunc="mean" and leave the gaps as NaN, then count them with .isna().sum().sum(). Passing fill_value would remove the very thing you are counting.

questions.prompt: What is a pivot table, in terms of what you already know?
choices: A two-key group-by laid out as a grid
questions.explain: Identical arithmetic, different shape — and the shape is the value, because a grid is scannable.
Which surprises people expecting a spreadsheet pivot’s count. Name it when you mean something else.

questions.prompt: A subject/year pair has no rows. What is in that cell?
questions.explain: Unlike a group-by, which omits the pair entirely, a grid has a cell for every combination.

questions.prompt: When is fill_value=0 the wrong choice?
questions.explain: It claims a group scored nothing when the truth is that nobody sat it. For a count, zero usually is the honest answer.
